title: Closures And Equivalence Classes
notes: Open by locating the section after the first pairing theorem for saddle-functions. The lecture is about what remains when the two natural closure procedures do not choose the same boundary values. Emphasize that the goal is a usable representative of a whole class, not a single formula memorized in isolation.

title: Two Closure Directions
notes: Start with a concave-convex saddle-function and name the two directions separately. Closing in the first variable repairs concave slices, while closing in the second variable repairs convex slices. The important point is that a two-step closure has an order, and Section 34 studies what that order remembers.

title: The First Stabilization
notes: Theorem 34.1 is a reassurance theorem. Once the lower closure is formed, applying the same lower-closure operation again does not keep changing the object; the same holds for the upper closure. The proof works by translating the saddle data through the associated bifunction and its adjoint.

title: A Corner Can Refuse A Value
notes: Use the corner picture as the first real warning. A boundary point may be approached in one order by fixing the convex variable and in the other order by fixing the concave variable. If those limiting stories disagree, no single corner value can satisfy both closure directions at once.

title: Effective Domain Is Product Data
notes: The effective domain definition is stricter than asking where a displayed formula is finite. The first domain keeps all second-variable slices above minus infinity; the second domain keeps all first-variable slices below plus infinity. Their product is the stable finite core used by the equivalence theory.

title: Equivalence And Closedness
notes: Equivalence means the two one-direction closures agree, not necessarily that the original functions agree at every boundary point. A closed saddle-function is one whose closures are already equivalent to it. This lets the theory keep boundary ambiguity while still having well-defined lower and upper representatives.

title: The Omega Of F Sandwich
notes: Theorem 34.2 is the organizing theorem. A closed convex bifunction supplies a lower member and an upper member, and every closed saddle-function in the class lies between them. The class is recovered from the sandwich, and the bifunction is recovered from any member by conjugate-type formulas.

title: Consequences Of The Sandwich
notes: Pause here to extract the practical conclusions before going into slice structure. Every proper class has one least lower closed member and one greatest upper closed member. If the bifunction is improper, the only closed saddle-functions left are the two constant infinities, which are not equivalent.

title: Slice Structure Of A Closed Class
notes: Theorem 34.3 is a diagnostic table. Interior slices are the clean case: closed proper convex or concave functions with the expected domain. Boundary slices can have domains between the original domain and its closure. Outside slices become improper, with infinity signs forced on the relative interior.

title: Kernel Determines The Class
notes: Now make the kernel the main invariant. Once the values are known on the relative interiors of the two domain factors, closedness forces the closures of all relevant slices. Theorem 34.4 says this finite interior saddle-function determines the entire proper closed equivalence class.

title: Simple Kernels Generate Classes
notes: The simple condition prevents slice domains from wandering beyond the closures of the intended factors. Theorem 34.5 then says the lower and upper closures of a proper simple saddle-function are equivalent, ordered, and form the endpoints of the class with the same kernel.

title: Recap
notes: Close by asking students to narrate the complete pipeline. Begin with a saddle-function, form the two ordered closures, detect possible boundary disagreement, pass to an equivalence class, read off its closed convex bifunction or kernel, and use the least and greatest representatives as the dependable endpoints.
